items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “A mood disorder with at least two weeks of depressed mood or loss of interest, plus other symptoms causing distress or impairment”.
items.answer: Major depressive disorder
items.markingKey: Major depressive disorder: a mood disorder with at least two weeks of depressed mood or loss of interest, plus other symptoms causing distress or impairment. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Bipolar II disorder involves hypomania rather than full mania. Reason (R): Hypomanic episodes are shorter and less severe than manic episodes. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: Bipolar II = hypomania plus major depressive episodes. [1]

items.stem: Describe the characteristics of a major depressive episode.
items.answer: Depressed mood and/or loss of interest or pleasure, with other symptoms such as weight or appetite change, insomnia or hypersomnia, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness or guilt, poor concentration and thoughts of death, for at least two weeks, causing distress or impairment.
items.markingKey: 1 mark core symptom; 1 mark further symptoms; 1 mark duration/impairment [3]

items.stem: For the last week Zara, from Jakarta, has slept only three hours a night, talked very fast, spent all their savings on plans to start five businesses and said they will become the richest person in the world. Explain why this episode could lead to a diagnosis of bipolar I rather than bipolar II.
items.answer: It lasts a week and causes marked impairment (spending all savings), which meets the criteria for a full manic episode rather than hypomania.
items.markingKey: 1 mark duration; 1 mark severity [2]

items.stem: For the last week Ethan, from Jakarta, has slept only three hours a night, talked very fast, spent all their savings on plans to start five businesses and said they will become the richest person in the world. (a) Explain why this episode could lead to a diagnosis of bipolar I rather than bipolar II. (b) Explain why it is important not to treat Ethan with antidepressants alone.
items.answer: (a) It lasts a week and causes marked impairment (spending all savings), which meets the criteria for a full manic episode rather than hypomania. (b) Antidepressants without a mood stabiliser can trigger or worsen manic episodes in people with bipolar disorder.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark duration; 1 mark severity [2] (b) 1 mark trigger mania; 1 mark need mood stabiliser [2]

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of the DSM-5 classification of mood disorders. Include at least one point about validity.
items.answer: Strength (reliability): Listing symptoms, a minimum number and a time period helps clinicians agree on a diagnosis of depression. Strength (usefulness): Distinguishing bipolar from unipolar depression matters because antidepressants alone can trigger mania in bipolar patients. Weakness (cultural differences): In some cultures depression is expressed mainly through physical complaints, so symptom-based criteria may miss it. Weakness (validity): Normal sadness after a loss may be diagnosed as depression, so the category may over-include ordinary experiences. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Evaluate Beck’s cognitive explanation of depression, including a discussion of supporting evidence.
items.answer: Strength (supporting evidence): Depressed people show more negative automatic thoughts and biased recall of negative information, as the theory predicts. Strength (usefulness): It led to CBT, which is an effective treatment for depression. Weakness (blame): By locating the problem in the person’s thinking, it may imply the patient is responsible and ignore real adverse circumstances. Weakness (cause and effect): Negative thinking may be a symptom of depression rather than its cause. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Evaluate Beck’s cognitive explanation of depression in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about usefulness.

items.stem: Explain Beck’s cognitive explanation of depression.

items.stem: Evaluate drug treatment (SSRIs) for depression in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about side effects.
items.answer: Strength (effectiveness): Many patients improve, and drugs can lift mood enough for them to engage with therapy. Strength (practicality): Drugs are cheap, widely available and need little time from professionals. Weakness (side effects): Side effects such as nausea, weight gain and sexual problems lead some patients to stop treatment. Weakness (placebo effects): Kirsch et al. found that much of the improvement also occurs with placebo, except in severe depression. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: “Drug treatment (SSRIs) for depression has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including placebo effects in your answer.

items.stem: Discuss the extent to which depression is best explained by cognitive factors.
items.answer: Arguments for: Beck’s cognitive triad and negative schemas explain the persistent negative thinking found in depressed people. CBT, based on cognitive theory, is an effective treatment. Learned helplessness explains passivity after uncontrollable events. Arguments against: Negative thinking may be a result, not a cause, of depression. Twin studies show a genetic component, and antidepressants that alter serotonin can reduce symptoms. Cognitive explanations neglect social causes such as poverty. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: A student writes: “The BDI can be used on its own to diagnose major depressive disorder.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. It measures severity of symptoms; diagnosis requires a clinical assessment against DSM-5 or ICD-11 criteria.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Jonas, a client at a clinic in Istanbul, completed the BDI-II (21 items, each scored 0–3). Item scores: 2, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 2, 2, 0. Calculate the total BDI-II score.
items.markingKey: Sum of the 21 item scores = 23. 1 mark working; 1 mark answer [2]

items.stem: Lina, a client at a clinic in Riyadh, completed the BDI-II (21 items, each scored 0–3). Item scores: 1, 2, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 3, 3, 3, 0, 3, 2, 3, 2, 2, 3. (a) Calculate the total BDI-II score. (b) Using the bands 0–13 minimal, 14–19 mild, 20–28 moderate and 29–63 severe, state the severity of depression indicated.
items.answer: (a) 45 (b) Severe (45)
items.markingKey: (a) Sum of the 21 item scores = 45. 1 mark working; 1 mark answer [2] (b) 45 falls in the severe band [1]

items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “A milder form of mania lasting at least four days that does not cause severe impairment”?
items.answer: Hypomania
items.markingKey: Hypomania: a milder form of mania lasting at least four days that does not cause severe impairment. [1]

items.stem: In a revision session, a student says: “Depression can include physical symptoms such as changes in sleep and appetite.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Somatic symptoms are part of the DSM-5 criteria.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: A clinic in Toronto compared BDI-II scores (0–63) after 12 weeks for 8 patients receiving CBT and 8 patients receiving an SSRI antidepressant. Table: BDI-II score after 12 weeks — CBT: 17, 9, 15, 21, 21, 18, 9, 24. SSRI: 20, 20, 19, 30, 21, 13, 22, 15. Calculate the percentage of participants in the SSRI condition who scored 20 or more. Show your working.
items.markingKey: 5 out of 8 participants scored 20 or more: 5 ÷ 8 × 100 = 62.5%. 1 mark working; 1 mark answer [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that depression is best explained by cognitive factors.
items.answer: Arguments for: Beck’s cognitive triad and negative schemas explain the persistent negative thinking found in depressed people. CBT, based on cognitive theory, is an effective treatment. Learned helplessness explains passivity after uncontrollable events. Arguments against: Negative thinking may be a result, not a cause, of depression. Twin studies show a genetic component, and antidepressants that alter serotonin can reduce symptoms. Cognitive explanations neglect social causes such as poverty. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: For the last week Noah, from Bogotá, has slept only three hours a night, talked very fast, spent all their savings on plans to start five businesses and said they will become the richest person in the world. (a) Identify two symptoms of mania shown by Noah. (b) Explain why this episode could lead to a diagnosis of bipolar I rather than bipolar II. (c) Explain why it is important not to treat Noah with antidepressants alone.
items.answer: (a) Decreased need for sleep; pressured speech; grandiosity; excessive risky activity (spending). (b) It lasts a week and causes marked impairment (spending all savings), which meets the criteria for a full manic episode rather than hypomania. (c) Antidepressants without a mood stabiliser can trigger or worsen manic episodes in people with bipolar disorder.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark duration; 1 mark severity [2] (c) 1 mark trigger mania; 1 mark need mood stabiliser [2]

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “Giving up trying to change a situation after repeated experience that one’s actions have no effect”?
items.answer: Learned helplessness
items.markingKey: Learned helplessness: giving up trying to change a situation after repeated experience that one’s actions have no effect. [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain Beck’s cognitive explanation of depression. (b) In a revision session, a student says: “Beck argued that depression is caused by low serotonin.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Negative schemas formed in childhood lead to automatic negative thoughts and cognitive biases (such as overgeneralisation); the person develops a negative triad about self, world and future, which maintains depression. (b) Not correct. Beck’s explanation is cognitive: faulty thinking and negative schemas.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark schemas; 1 mark triad; 1 mark biases/automatic thoughts [3] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the biochemical explanation of depression. (b) A student writes: “Learned helplessness was first demonstrated in research with animals.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Depression is linked to low activity of monoamines such as serotonin and noradrenaline; antidepressants that increase their availability reduce symptoms. (b) Correct. Seligman and Maier (1967) used dogs given inescapable shocks.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark low monoamines; 1 mark evidence from drugs [2] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Yusuf, a student in Accra, failed one exam and now says: “I’m useless at everything. Nothing will ever go right for me, and everyone thinks I’m a failure.” Explain Yusuf’s attributional style using the learned helplessness model.
items.answer: The failure is attributed internally (my fault), stably (always) and globally (everything), which leads to hopelessness and passivity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark internal/stable/global; 1 mark consequence [2]

items.stem: Tariq compared depression scores (BDI-II, 0–63) after 12 weeks for patients randomly allocated to CBT or to an SSRI. Table: BDI-II score after 12 weeks — CBT: 18, 17, 12, 10, 18, 8. SSRI: 21, 30, 22, 21, 17, 24. Explain one ethical issue that the researcher should consider in this study.
items.answer: Patients must be monitored for suicidal thoughts and given help if needed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: ethical guideline named; 1 mark: applied to this study [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Riyadh is interested in whether a short course of CBT reduces negative automatic thoughts in students with low mood. Design a field experiment to test this. Your plan must include: ethical issues, how the dependent variable will be measured and the sampling technique.
items.answer: Method: a field experiment. Manipulate the IV in a natural everyday setting; participants may not know they are being studied; standardise as much of the procedure as possible. Variables: IV: CBT course or waiting list; DV: number of negative thoughts recorded in a diary. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Riyadh, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: Define the term ‘rational emotive behaviour therapy (REBT)’.
items.answer: Ellis’s therapy in which irrational beliefs are disputed and replaced with rational ones.
items.markingKey: Rational emotive behaviour therapy (REBT): Ellis’s therapy in which irrational beliefs are disputed and replaced with rational ones. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: In a revision session, a student says: “CBT involves homework tasks between sessions.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Clients practise recording and challenging thoughts and scheduling activities.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain one weakness of drug treatment (SSRIs) for depression in terms of long-term outcome.
items.answer: They do not teach coping skills, so relapse rates after stopping may be higher than after CBT.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to long-term outcome; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Chloe, from Lisbon, became depressed after losing a job and believes: “I must be successful at everything or I am worthless.” Suggest how an REBT therapist would dispute Chloe’s belief.
items.answer: Ask for evidence that failing at one job makes a person worthless, point out that the “must” is illogical, and help replace it with “I would prefer to succeed, but failing does not make me worthless.”
items.markingKey: 1 mark disputing technique; 1 mark rational alternative [2]

items.stem: Mateo compared depression scores (BDI-II, 0–63) after 12 weeks for patients randomly allocated to CBT or to an SSRI. Table: BDI-II score after 12 weeks — CBT: 13, 15, 11, 28, 16, 22. SSRI: 15, 26, 27, 28, 23, 25. (a) Calculate the mean score for each condition. Give your answers to one decimal place. (b) Describe one variable that should be controlled in this study and explain why.
items.answer: (a) CBT: 17.5; SSRI: 24.0. (b) The same assessor, who does not know the treatment group, for all patients.
items.markingKey: (a) CBT: 105 ÷ 6 = 17.5; SSRI: 144 ÷ 6 = 24.0. 1 mark for each correct mean [2] (b) 1 mark: relevant control identified; 1 mark: explains how it would otherwise act as a confounding variable [2]

items.stem: In a revision session, a student says: “Each BDI item is scored from 0 to 3.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Higher scores indicate more severe symptoms.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Mei compared depression scores (BDI-II, 0–63) after 12 weeks for patients randomly allocated to CBT or to an SSRI. Table: BDI-II score after 12 weeks — CBT: 17, 13, 17, 17, 6, 10, 24. SSRI: 22, 11, 17, 24, 16, 20, 17. Name the experimental design used in this study and explain one weakness of using this design here.
items.answer: Independent measures: different participants take part in each condition. Weakness: participant variables (individual differences between the two groups) may explain the difference in the DV instead of the IV.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct design; 1 mark: weakness explained in context [2]

items.stem: Priya, a client at a clinic in Manila, completed the BDI-II (21 items, each scored 0–3). Item scores: 1, 0, 3, 2, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 3. (a) Using the bands 0–13 minimal, 14–19 mild, 20–28 moderate and 29–63 severe, state the severity of depression indicated. (b) After eight weeks of CBT, Priya’s total was 20. Calculate the percentage reduction in score.
items.markingKey: (a) 31 falls in the severe band [1] (b) (31 − 20) ÷ 31 × 100 = 35.5%. 1 mark working; 1 mark answer [2]
